Category Growth Diagnostic · Storage & Organisers · Noon AE

The category is growing on traffic —
and quietly losing it on conversion.

GMV is up +47.7% YoY (Aug'26 vs Aug'25, both full months) on a genuinely broad base — traffic is doing most of the work, with pricing/AOV contributing too. But the most recent month breaks that pattern: in the last 31 days, three of the category's biggest subcategories — Storage Box, Racks, Storage Basket — suffered a sudden conversion crash with no precedent anywhere in the prior 19 months of data, and it's still live as of the latest data.

Periods: Jan 2025 – Aug 2026, continuous, 20 months YoY: Aug'26 vs Aug'25 (both full months) · MoM: Aug'26 vs Jul'26 Rows analysed: 735,639 SKU-months Prepared for: Category Manager, Storage & Organisers
Data note — read before the numbers below. Source data is now continuous from Jan 2025 to Aug 2026 (20 months, no gaps), and Aug'26 is now a full 31-day month — every monthly figure uses the same daily-rate, month-equivalent run-rate (×30.4) for comparability across months of different lengths. Because Aug'26 is now complete, headline YoY figures use the current month directly (Aug'26 vs Aug'25), with Aug'26 vs Jul'26 as the MoM lens for what's happening most recently. As of this refresh, scope also includes Laundry Care — a separate `pt` in the source data, not previously pulled into this dashboard — alongside Storage & Home Organization; see §00.2. No competitor, ad-spend/ROAS, or ratings/reviews data exists in the source — those sections are flagged as data gaps rather than estimated.

00.1

Where the GMV opportunity sits

Every number below is quantified from the data, not extrapolated from a trend line. Ranges reflect immediate (vs last month) to fuller recovery-to-recent-normal benchmarks.

Biggest single lever
AED 440K–480K /mo
Conversion recovery in Storage Boxes, Racks & Storage Baskets — each was stable for 19 straight months, then crashed 0.6–3.4 CVR points in the single most recent month, with no precedent in the prior data. See §02, §05, §14 Action 1.
Second lever
AED 535K /mo
Click-through gap in 9 subcategories (Clothes Drying Stand, Food Containers, Hangers, Lunch Boxes/Bags…) — CTR well below 4.24% category avg on healthy impression volume. See §05, §14 Action 2.
Third lever
AED 433K–531K /mo
Lost GMV to OOS, concentrated in Express fulfilment — real fields in the data, not modelled. See §10, §14 Action 4–5.

Gross identified opportunity across all P0–P2 actions: ~AED 1.6M/mo. A realistic, execution-adjusted capture in the first two quarters is ~AED 550–650K/mo, scaling toward the full figure as fulfilment and assortment actions land (§13, §15).

02

Subcategory Growth Matrix

51 subcategories (pst) — now including Laundry Care's 7 subcategories alongside the 44 Storage & Home Organization ones (§00.2). Growth and contribution use the clean YoY comparison (Aug'26 vs Aug'25, both full months) — the metric that matters for prioritisation, not % growth on a small base.

All 51 subcategories by absolute GMV contribution to YoY category growth
Winning, and why

Storage Box (+104% YoY, +AED 240K/mo) and Space Saver Bag (+253% YoY, +AED 219K/mo) remain the two biggest growth drivers. But Clothes Drying Stand — Laundry Care's largest subcategory — is now the #4 subcategory in the whole category by GMV (AED 395K/mo, +28% YoY), bigger than Space Saver Bag; Iron Board (AED 174K/mo, +33% YoY) and Laundry Hamper (AED 114K/mo, +77% YoY) are also solidly growing. Space Saver Bag is growing on both volume and price — ASP up 43% YoY while still gaining share. Bag (+289%) and Foldable Wardrobe (+235%) show the same pattern: real demand, not promo-fuelled.

Declining, and why

Closet Organization Systems (−29% YoY, −AED 19K/mo), Kitchen Storage Accessories (−53%) and Cabinet/Drawer Organization (−3%, −AED 4K/mo) are down on weak CTR (§05) rather than price or stock. Within Laundry Care, Laundry Basket (−40% YoY, −AED 28K/mo) and Laundry Bag (−55% YoY) are the category's two sharpest decliners — both losing share to the newer, better-converting Laundry Hamper pst (see above), which looks like an internal cannibalisation/relisting pattern rather than falling demand for laundry storage overall.

03.1 · Which price point wins — by subcategory (this year only)

Jun–Aug 2026 combined (the most recent complete quarter, 2026 data only — not blended with 2025) so this reflects current buying behaviour, not last year's. "Wins" = highest GMV, not highest CVR — cheap items convert better almost by definition, so a CVR-ranked winner would just point at the entry band every time and say nothing about where the money actually is. All 41 subcategories with meaningful volume (including Laundry Care's Clothes Drying Stand, Iron Board and Laundry Hamper — its smaller subcategories fall below the AED 500/mo threshold here); CVR shown alongside for reference only.

SubcategoryHighest-GMV bandGMV there% of its totalCVR there

Read as "where the money already is" — for buying/assortment decisions, not conversion tuning. 50–100 AED is the GMV centre of gravity for half the category (20 of 40 subcategories), typically 40–60% of a group's total GMV in a single band — this is the tier to protect stock depth and price competitiveness in first. A handful of subcategories peak elsewhere for structural reasons: Bag and Aluminium Foil skew to <25 AED (low-ASP by nature), Foldable Wardrobe and Garage Storage to 100–200 AED (bulky/durable goods), and Cooler/Outdoor Storage to 400+ AED (premium, low-frequency purchases) — buying into those categories at entry price would miss where their demand actually sits.

04

Seller Analysis

Seller concentration (2,185 active sellers)
SBB sellers cancel 13.5% of GMV — 4–6× the FBN (2.3%), Retail (2.4%) and DSE (3.4%) rates, on only 3.3% of category GMV. Not a scale risk, but a concrete, fixable CX/recovery item. See Action 8 (§14).

Seller concentration itself is healthy — the top seller (noon Retail) holds 24.8%, top 10 hold 45.7%, top 20 hold 54.8% — no single-seller dependency risk. FBN (Fulfilled by Noon marketplace) is the dominant model at 63.7% share with the best cancellation profile, though its standard instock (90.8%) now trails DSE and SBB (§04.1) — a fulfilment-depth issue, not a seller-quality one.

04.1 · Business model hierarchy — testing Retail > FBN > DSE > SBB

Testing the hypothesis directly: the clean hierarchy doesn't hold. SBB is still unambiguously the floor on cancellations (13.5% vs 2.3–3.4% for the other three, an even wider gap than last cycle) and roughly ties DSE for weakest Express readiness — but it's no longer the floor on standard instock: Retail is (84.4%, now below SBB's 92.7%). Conversion has flipped too: only Retail clearly out-converts the rest now (7.18%); SBB's CVR (3.75%) has fallen to roughly FBN/DSE levels, so SBB's problem is no longer just fulfilment execution sitting on top of strong demand — its conversion has weakened as well.

Business modelGMV/moGMV ShareYoYImpressionsCVRASPInstock%Express Instock%Cancel%Return%SellersSKUs
Instock % — Retail is now the floor on standard instock; SBB stays the floor on cancellations
Reversed from last cycle: Retail (84.4%) is now the standard-instock floor, not SBB (92.7%) — a genuine flip, not a rounding difference. Standard instock: DSE (93.4%) > SBB (92.7%) > FBN (90.8%) > Retail (84.4%). Express instock: FBN (86.2%) > Retail (82.4%) > DSE (76.4%) > SBB (72.9%) — SBB and DSE are both weak on Express readiness, essentially tied at the bottom. Cancellation is still the one metric where SBB is unambiguously worst, by an even wider margin than before: FBN (2.3%) ≈ Retail (2.4%) < DSE (3.4%) <<< SBB (13.5%). SBB remains structurally the weakest channel on cancellations specifically — but it's no longer the clean "floor on everything" story.
The proof, at SKU level: same product, different channel
CHAKO LAB stainless-steel vacuum tumbler (Food Containers) sells through both FBN and DSE simultaneously. Its FBN listings: AED 1,043 combined GMV, zero cancellations. Its DSE listings: AED 2,515 combined GMV, AED 596 cancelled (24%) — one DSE listing sits at just 42% instock. Identical product, channel is the only variable.
MACKENZIE-CHILDS enamel pot (Storage Set): the SBB-fulfilled listing had its entire AED 593 order cancelled outright, while its two FBN-fulfilled sibling listings (canisters from the same brand) sold cleanly with zero cancellations.

05

Funnel Diagnosis

Impressions → Search Impressions → GV → ATC → Units → GMV, category-wide, Aug'26 vs Jul'26.

Funnel step change, MoM

Leak point: GV→ATC (add-to-cart rate) fell 1.44pp (18.74%→17.31%) even as GV surged — new traffic is browsing but adding to cart at a lower rate, and what does get added converts to orders worse too (CVR −0.62pp). The funnel is wider at the top and leakier in the middle simultaneously.

How to read the table below
Each row's Issue is the weak stage vs category benchmark. Cause is checked, not assumed — MoM instock and price moves are tested before defaulting to "listing/execution." Click a row for the worst offending brand, exact SKUs, and the action to take.
05.1 · $ opportunity by subcategory — issue, cause & action (Aug'26)
SubcategoryGMV/moIssue (vs category)CauseOpp./mo
05.2 · The funnel, drawn — and exactly where each stage leaks
How to fix each stage — three separate levers, three separate teams
↑ Increase GV (traffic)

Fix CTR, not impressions — impression volume is already healthy in every problem subcat. Rewrite titles/thumbnails for noon_east and milton first (highest absolute impression waste); run a search-relevance/keyword audit on the 9 CTR-problem subcats. Not a paid-ads fix. ≈ AED 535K/mo (§13).

↑ Increase ATC

ATC-rate loss is 95% concentrated in Storage Box and Storage Basket specifically — Racks' issue has shifted to conversion (see CVR lever) rather than add-to-cart, but all three are the same August event, not a separate PDP problem elsewhere. Audit primary image, price badge and size/spec clarity on the highest-GV SKUs in Storage Box and Storage Basket first.

↑ Increase CVR

Start with the dish-drying-rack duplicate-listing cluster inside Racks (§07) — 6 near-identical SKUs converting 0–2% on real traffic. Then verify no price/stock sync fault broke checkout for Storage Box and Storage Basket specifically in the last cycle.

Winsor and Vileda are pulling away. Winsor holds 23.2% share (+7.5pp vs H1'25) and Vileda 16.1% (+6.8pp) — together 39% of the subcategory on just 16 SKUs combined, both gaining share while running a much leaner assortment than the branded leaders in Storage Box/Racks. Share gainers, and why

Duniso is the standout — #1 in Storage Box (23.1% share, +11.5pp) and a top-3 gainer in Racks (+6.9pp) and Storage Basket. Broad-based, multi-subcategory share gain at low ASP (AED 20–171/SKU) — a value/generic-tier consolidator winning on assortment breadth and price, not a single hero SKU. In Laundry Care, Winsor and Vileda show the same pattern one subcategory over.

Share losers, and why

Cosmoplast (storage box, −29pp) and Generic-tagged listings in Racks (−8.6pp) are the largest losers. Generic's loss is structural — branded/named sellers (Duniso, Toshionics, Auraluxi) are displacing unbranded listings as the mix professionalises. Cosmoplast's loss is a visibility incident, not competitive displacement (see above) — different root cause, different fix. Royalford in Clothes Drying Stand (−8.7pp) is the same generic-displacement pattern.

Food Containers carries the deepest brand roster in the category (488 brands, 4,555 SKUs) for the 5th-highest GMV — the most assortment-crowded subcategory relative to its sales, and the clearest rationalization target alongside Racks (378 brands) and Lunch Box (378 brands). Laundry Care's brand rosters are comparatively tight by contrast — Clothes Drying Stand (#4 by GMV) runs only 201 brands, a much cleaner assortment than Storage's top tier.

Over-assorted (rationalize)

Selling-SKU rate actually improved from 29.9% (FY25 H1) to 33.3% (Aug'26) even as total listings grew 37% — the catalog isn't outrunning demand on average. But the absolute dead-stock pool is still large and concentrated: Food Containers (3,146 zero-sale SKUs), Racks (2,565) and Storage Box (1,849) hold the biggest pools and are worth a targeted rationalization pass regardless of the improving average. See §14 Action 10.

Under-assorted (evidenced demand)

200–400 & 400+ AED bands: GV growth YoY of +77% and +26% against only 18–22% selling-SKU rate — and for 200–400 AED specifically, the category's single weakest instock score (85.2%, well below every other band). This is a demand-first signal (not a guess) — concentrated in Racks, Clothes Rack and Cabinet/Drawer Organization, where a handful of premium SKUs (esqube, teuuea) already prove the tier works. Directional opportunity: AED 80–120K/mo, low confidence pending a curated test. See §14 Action 7.

Data gap: no competitor price, assortment or ranking data exists in the source files, so white-space sizing above is demand-led (internal GV/instock/SKU-count signals only) and cannot be cross-checked against competitor assortment or pricing. Treat all §04 and §08 figures as internal-signal estimates.
08.1 · Cannibalization check
No subcategory-level evidence. Checked whether selling-SKU count grew faster than GMV MoM (a proxy for demand being split across more listings rather than genuinely growing) across all 51 subcategories — zero show that pattern in the latest month, Laundry Care included. Category growth in §02 is not an artifact of catalog inflation.
Brand × SubcatSKUsSelling%GMV/moGMV/SKU

But real risk exists within specific brands. dubaigallery in Racks runs 642 SKUs for just AED 38/SKU/mo (11.2% selling) and locknlock in Food Containers runs 347 SKUs for AED 26/SKU/mo (24.2% selling) — assortment sprawl broad enough that near-duplicate listings are very likely splitting the same search traffic against each other rather than capturing incremental demand. The same brand shows the identical pattern in Laundry Care: dubaigallery also runs 32 SKUs in Laundry Hamper with zero selling — a fully dead sub-assortment, not a slow one. Worth a listing-consolidation review before adding any more SKUs to any of these.

Bentgo (Lunch Box) returns 25% of its GMV — the single worst brand-level return rate in the category, on a real base (AED 5.5K/mo). Chako_lab cancels 15.3% (matches its DSE/SBB exposure above, §04.1). The pattern is consistent: small, low-diversification brands leaning on weaker fulfilment channels show up on every quality metric, not just one. Likely root causes from the data available: returns cluster in bulky/assembly-heavy or fragile-item PSTs (Cube Shelf, Cooler, Bread Box — consistent with fit/assembly or damage-in-transit issues, not confirmable without a returns-reason field); cancellations cluster in the same small-brand, SBB/DSE-heavy names — a fulfilment-capacity issue, not a demand issue. Laundry Care is notably clean on both metrics — none of its 7 subcategories or their top brands appear in either top-8 list above; its return/cancel profile tracks the category average rather than standing out as a quality problem.

Organic CTR by subcategory — category average 4.24% — now including Laundry Care's top 3 subcategories
Discount depth vs conversion — Aug'26
Light discounting helps, deeper discounting doesn't add more. 1–10% discount converts best (6.0%) — clearly above no discount at all (5.0%). But every tier beyond that (11–50%+) converts at 4.3–4.9%, below the 1–10% tier and not improving with more discount depth (now including Laundry Care's own discount mix). Deeper discounting is not evidenced to drive incremental conversion beyond the 1–10% level; it looks like it's mostly applied to weaker SKUs, not used to unlock demand. Recommendation: don't expand discount past ~10% as a blanket lever — see Action 9 (§14).

Seasonality

12.1 · Monthly GMV & Units — 2025 vs 2026, YoY

Same monthly-equivalent series as the chart above, laid out month-by-month with YoY next to each — GMV and Units. 2026 is complete only through Aug — Sep–Dec 2026 will fill in as those months close.

Month2025 GMV/mo2026 GMV/moGMV YoY %2025 Units/mo2026 Units/moUnits YoY %

Aug'26 is still the highest month in the entire series (AED 4.23M/mo) — well above the Jan–Mar 2026 Ramadan cluster (AED 3.44M–3.48M/mo, essentially flat across all three months), which is itself the clearest seasonal event: Feb–Mar 2026 squarely matches Ramadan 2026 (~Feb 18–Mar 19). Aug'26's level is best read as continued structural growth (§01), not a seasonal spike — August carries no obvious seasonal driver in this category. Holiday-season effect — now the strongest read in 2025: with Laundry Care in the mix, Nov–Dec 2025 is 2025's actual peak (AED 3.23M and 3.24M/mo), edging out Aug'25 (AED 2.86M) — Laundry Care's own Nov–Dec skew (Clothes Drying Stand and Iron Board both peak into year-end, §02) is what pulls the combined category's holiday season above its August level, a pattern invisible in the narrower Storage-only view. Summer trough: both years dip hardest in Jun (2025: AED 2.14M, the 2025 low; 2026: AED 2.90M, a much shallower dip given underlying YoY growth, followed by Aug'26's sharp rebound). Every single month from Aug'25 onward sits above its Jan–Jul'25 counterpart-period level, reinforcing that the growth in §01 is structural, not just riding these seasonal cycles.

15

Category Growth Plan

A · Diagnosis — what is happening

Storage & Organisers (including Laundry Care) is in genuine, broad-based growth — GMV is up 47.7% YoY (Aug'26 vs Aug'25, both full months) and 36.1% MoM, with traffic doing most of the work and pricing/AOV contributing too. That healthy picture broke in the most recent month: three subcategories that together carry 23.5% of category GMV — Storage Box, Racks, Storage Basket — each had a sudden conversion crash with no precedent in the prior 19 months of stable data, and add-to-cart rate fell 1.44pp MoM even as visits surged.

B · Root causes — why

Three distinct, independently-evidenced mechanisms: (1) a genuine conversion-quality problem concentrated in a handful of high-visit subcategories and SKU clusters (e.g. duplicate dish-rack listings) — not price-driven, since discount depth shows no CVR benefit anywhere in the category; (2) a discoverability/CTR gap in nine mid-size subcategories that sit on healthy impression volume but convert those impressions to visits poorly, pointing at title/thumbnail/search-relevance rather than demand; (3) operational leakage — chronic OOS concentrated in a short list of SKUs and specifically in Express fulfilment (79.7% vs 91.7% instock), plus one clear brand-visibility incident (Cosmoplast) that looks like a listing/ranking fault, not competitive loss.

C · Biggest growth pools — where
D · The 5–10 things to do next

In order: fix conversion in the Big 3 subcategories (§14 Action 1); close the CTR gap in the nine mid-size subcategories (Action 2); recover Cosmoplast's lost visibility (Action 3); clear the top-15 chronic-OOS SKU list and the Express fulfilment gap (Actions 4–5); protect the Space Saver Bag / Storage Box breakout without discounting (Action 6); test premium price-band assortment in Racks-adjacent subcategories (Action 7); fix SBB seller cancellations (Action 8); stop expanding discount depth (Action 9); and rationalize the 25K-SKU zero-sales tail to fund the above (Action 10). Full detail, evidence and owners for each are in §14.

Confidence & scope statement. All GMV estimates hold current traffic, price and mix structure constant and isolate one lever at a time — they are not additive guarantees, and real-world capture will be lower than the gross sum due to execution friction and interaction effects between levers (e.g. fixing CTR raises the traffic base the conversion fix acts on, which is directionally positive but not modelled here). Treat the ~AED 550–650K/mo two-quarter capture estimate in §00 as the operating target, and the ~AED 1.6M/mo gross figure as the multi-quarter ceiling.
